title: Cyrus and the Inventory
premise: Mara Yarrow has spent a decade mailing postcards to her childhood home, destroyed in a fire that took her grandmother and, with it, the family's true name. When a stranger named Cyrus appears at her mother's funeral and calls the family by their old surname, Mara discovers her grandmother had another child — a son she gave up, who has returned with a terminal diagnosis and a box of unsent letters. Forced to share a house and a history with the stranger she has every reason to resent, Mara must decide whether the family she curated in grief is worth more than the one she could still have. The novel ends with Cyrus's death in early spring, after which Mara finally stops mailing the postcards and instead opens a shop that sells paper, ink, and second chances to strangers writing their own.
about_author: Ulyana Iversen is the pen name of a former estate-sale appraiser who spent years cataloguing the belongings of the recently departed. Her fiction explores the objects and names people leave behind. She writes from a coastal town whose name she declines to confirm.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. At her mother's sparsely attended funeral, Mara performs her practiced grief, deflecting condolences with a smile that closes doors. A postcard in her coat pocket, addressed to a burned-down house, hints at her private ritual. The emotional beat is controlled loneliness — a woman who has mistaken silence for peace.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A stranger named Cyrus approaches the graveside and says a surname Mara has never heard — her grandmother's maiden name, or so he claims. He leaves before she can question him, dropping a photograph of three children, one of them Mara's mother, one of them him. The beat: the ground shifts under a life built on a curated past.

chapters.title: What the Fire Kept
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with a flashback to age eleven. Mara searches the storage unit holding her grandmother's salvaged belongings and finds a locked tin and a hospital bracelet with the unfamiliar name. Flashback reveals the fire and the first postcard she ever sent. The beat: grief's architecture examined, and found to have a hidden room.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Old Photographs
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus, ill and running out of time, explains why he came: he is the child his grandmother gave away, and he wants not money but the truth of why. Mara refuses him coldly, but takes the photograph. The beat: resentment meeting vulnerability, neither willing to blink first.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Locked Tin
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The tin yields unsent letters from her grandmother to the adopted-away son, spanning thirty years, each one ending mid-apology. Mara reads them all night, furious at the dead woman and at herself for wanting to forgive her. The beat: anger as a form of love with nowhere to go.

chapters.title: Terms of Occupancy
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Cyrus, hospitalized briefly, needs a place to recover; Mara, against her better judgment, offers her spare room — framed as pragmatism. They negotiate house rules like hostile nations signing a treaty. Small comic warmth breaks through. The beat: two lonely people building a fragile, unspoken truce.

chapters.title: Postcards, Undelivered
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Cyrus discovers her decade of postcards to the burned house and, instead of mocking her, asks to help write the next one. They compose it together — the first honest letter Mara has written in years. The beat: confession disguised as collaboration; the ritual loosens its grip.

chapters.title: The Last Address
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus's condition worsens; he asks Mara to find the family that raised him and deliver a letter she was never meant to read — one revealing the grandmother searched for him for years and was turned away. Mara's resentment collapses into grief. The beat: forgiveness arriving too late to be spoken, in time to be felt.

chapters.title: Everything the House Remembered
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Climax. Cyrus comes home to die. Mara reads him the grandmother's final unsent letter aloud, finishing the apology she never completed. He dies at dawn holding the photograph of the three children. The beat: the family, whole at last for one impossible hour.

chapters.title: Open for Business
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, one year later. Mara mails the final postcard — to Cyrus's grave, this time — and unlocks a new shop selling paper, ink, and letter-writing desks. On the wall hangs the photograph of three children, all of them named. The beat: belonging chosen rather than inherited; an ending that is a beginning.
